bottleneck: Editing the human germline would permanently alter inheritance, yet no international consensus exists on safety thresholds, oversight, or permissible indications. Technical immaturity compounds the ethics: off-target edits and mosaicism in embryos could propagate unknown defects for generations, and candidate gene functions are incompletely understood, so consequences cannot be modeled in advance. The 2018 He Jiankui case showed the field cannot currently self-police, and every nation sets its own rules.
current_state: Most nations ban or heavily restrict heritable editing while research continues on non-viable embryos and animal models. Governance frameworks remain fragmented and advisory rather than binding, with no enforcement mechanism for cross-border violations.

title: No safe framework for heritable human genome editing
why_it_blocks: Without a credible path to safe, governed germline editing, humanity cannot eliminate inherited disease at its source. The stalemate also stalls legitimate research, since unclear rules deter careful scientists alongside rogue experiments, freezing the entire field.
